https://www.hulldailymail.co.uk/news/hul.text: A violent and abusive bully made a woman's life a "misery" – and left her feeling "worthless" – after a "relentless" campaign of nasty and intimidating behaviour towards her. Robert Szymske caused her to suffer a "nightmare" and it was deliberately "intended to grind her down" and "belittle" her, a court heard. Szymske, 49, of Porter Street, west Hull, but recently in custody on remand, denied a series of offences, including controlling and coercive behaviour between December 29, 2015 and July 16 last year but he was convicted by a jury at Grimsby Crown Court after a trial. He was also convicted of intentional strangulation on April 18 last year and perverting the course of justice between April 20 and July 16 last year. Judge Richard Woolfall told a sentencing hearing at Hull Crown Court that the violence against the woman included Szymske grabbing her in a headlock during one argument and applying pressure for a few seconds, restricting her breathing. He was violent and made threats of violence throughout their relationship as well as being abusive and intimidating. The last three or four years of the relationship were the worst. Judge Woolfall told Szymske: "It was almost daily when you subjected her to that sort of behaviour, which had a very significant impact on her health. "Your behaviour was deliberate and it was intended to cause distress and fear and intended to grind her down, which it did. It was relentless in the way you belittled her. You just kept on going." Szymske later sent messages in a bid to try to get the woman to withdraw her account. He made threats and was "trying to use that as a lever" to drop her claims against him. "The impact on her has been very significant," said Judge Woolfall. "You made her feel so worthless that she ultimately became too frightened to leave you. "The life inside that household was one of misery. Fear of harm was caused on many occasions." The woman said in a statement that the behaviour of Szymske took a toll on her whole life and she felt trapped. "Robert caused me to feel worthless," she said. "I didn't feel important enough to seek help. I consider my relationship with Robert to be a nightmare. "My relationship with Robert is still casting a shadow over my life. I feel free, free of arguments, free of misunderstandings." Claire Holmes, mitigating, said that Szymske felt real remorse, even though he did not accept all the allegations made against him. He wished to communicate his sadness and regret and he was apologetic. There were green shoots in his attitude that might lead to change in the future. Szymske, from Poland, was likely to be deported. "He has already received papers regarding deportation," said Miss Holmes. "He has been in this country for 20 years. He has built a life here." He had no previous convictions. Szymske was jailed for eight-and-a-half years. He was given an indefinite restraining order. https://www.dailykos.com/stories/2026/8/.text: Daily Kos Community Kitchen Table Kibitzing August 9, 2026 by side pocket Community This content is not subject to review by Daily Kos staff prior to publication. August 9, 2026 at 5:30 PM Recommend Story Share: Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Share on Bluesky (Opens in new window) Bluesky Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share using Native tools Share Copied to clipboard Save 79 Comments Add Daily Kos to Google KTK belinda ridgewood Climate Change and me We are aware of the heat domes affecting much of the U S. Affecting us less is the unusual and mostly unprecedented heat in Europe. France, Spain and Greece battle wildfires as Europe swelters . I have been reading stories about low water levels in the rivers. Across Europe, there are about 41,000 kilometres of navigable rivers and canals. These waterways connect cities, ports and industrial areas and are a key aspect for economic development. They are especially useful for transporting heavy goods such as coal, steel, chemicals or grain. There are other ways of transporting goods, such as trains and trucks, but I read that there are some items, such as big generators and industrial parts, can only be transported by river. Another concern is cooling for nuclear generation. Much of Europe’s existing nuclear fleet was designed around historical ranges of water temperature and flow that are becoming less dependable. YouTube has been sending me these stories for a reason. As most of you know, we are scheduled for a Viking Rhine River trip in October. The big story for the public is the low water level especially on the Rhine, Europe’s most important waterway. Daily I receive YouTube stories of cancelled or interrupted trips. When a portion of a river is not navigable, travelers are bussed instead, which makes for a very expensive bus vacation. We have travel insurance, but refunds might not be what we expect; vouchers instead of refunds. This trip was pricy and likely the last one I’ll be able to manage, given my spinal stenosis. Many of the videos advise waiting and watching the weather. And most say “go with the flow, you’ll have fun anyway.” Our trip, Paris to Prague is 100% booked, so we’re not alone. And since this is KTK, every river trip video confirms, all the food is fabulous and over the top. https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/n.text: ‘A story about how little we sometimes know the very people we love most’… Patrick Radden Keefe. Photograph: Maria Spann/The Guardian View image in fullscreen ‘A story about how little we sometimes know the very people we love most’… Patrick Radden Keefe. Photograph: Maria Spann/The Guardian Books Patrick Radden Keefe’s London Falling named Waterstones book of the year The word-of-mouth success of the journalist’s investigation into the death of a London teenager is ‘one of the defining features of the literary year’ Emma Loffhagen Wed 25 Nov 2026 19.01 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google London Falling, Patrick Radden Keefe’s bestselling investigation into the mysterious death of a London teenager, has been named Waterstones book of the year. View image in fullscreen The book follows the parents of Zac Brettler, a 19-year-old who fell from the balcony of a luxury London apartment after pretending to be the son of a wealthy Russian oligarch, as they discover the murky, dangerous underworld of the city that their son had been drawn into. In a Guardian review, Ian Thomson called it “a scrupulously researched work of narrative nonfiction”. “Grimly absorbing from start to finish,” he wrote, the book “opens a window on to a world of financial dirty work and Walter Mitty-like fantasies of aspirational wealth.” Waterstones’ head of books, Bea Carvalho, said its word-of-mouth success “has been one of the defining features of the literary year”. Reading nonfiction is “vital, enriching, gripping and the buzz surrounding London Falling has helped so many readers discover this,” she added. View image in fullscreen Radden Keefe, a staff writer at the New Yorker whose previous book Empire of Pain won the Baillie Gifford prize, said that at heart London Falling “is a story about family – about parents and children, about the perils of contemporary adolescence, and about how little we sometimes know the very people we love most”. The book was shortlisted for this year’s Baillie Gifford prize. Meanwhile, Taiwan Travelogue by Yáng Shuāng-zǐ, translated by Lin King, which won the International Booker prize earlier this year, was named fiction book of the year. Yáng said it was “especially precious to see this story about Taiwan embraced and adored by the booksellers at Waterstones”. Is This a Plum? by Oscar-nominated director Dan Ojari and his eight-year-old son, Finn, was named children’s book of the year. The cut-out picture book began when the pair realised “a plum looks a lot like a hippo’s bum”, said Dan. “Me and my dad made this book together – it’s very easy to read and will probably make you laugh at least once,” added Finn. View image in fullscreen The winners will receive the “full and committed backing of Waterstones shops and booksellers across the UK”, according to the company. Also on the shortlist were Yesteryear by Caro Claire Burke , Stations by Louise Kennedy , The Book of Birds by Robert Macfarlane and Jackie Morris , Redwood by Ben Macintyre , Land by Maggie O’Farrell , May We Feed the King by Rebecca Perry , Ottolenghi Simple Too by Yotam Ottolenghi and Verena Lochmuller, The Things We Never Say by Elizabeth Strout and John of John by Douglas Stuart , among others. Both the shortlisted titles and the book of the year are nominated and chosen by a panel of Waterstones booksellers. Last year’s winner was The Artist by Lucy Steeds, while The Café at the Edge of the Woods by Mikey Please was named children’s book of the year.
